questions.stem: A 420 N equipment case rests on a level floor. If the coefficient of friction is 0.28, what horizontal force is required to just overcome friction?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: For a level surface, the normal force equals the weight. Frictional force is F = mu*N = 0.28*420 N = 117.6 N.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This multiplies the weight by 0.20 rather than the stated coefficient.
This value does not result from multiplying the normal force by 0.28.
This treats the full normal force as friction and ignores the coefficient.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)

questions.stem: A 18 kg inspection cart is moving at 4.0 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
incorrectOptionExplanations: This omits half of the squared-velocity contribution.
This doubles the correct result after calculating m*v^2.
This multiplies mass by velocity squared without the one-half factor.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); NIST Joule definition
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 17, Kinetic Energy, pp. 454-455; NIST, joule as one newton-meter of work

questions.stem: A 32 kg tool chest is lifted 2.5 m onto a platform. Using g = 9.8 m/s^2, how much gravitational potential energy is added?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Potential energy is PE = m*g*h = 32*9.8*2.5 = 784 J.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This multiplies mass by height but omits gravitational acceleration.
This uses an incorrect gravitational acceleration of 8 m/s^2.
This multiplies mass and height by an unsupported factor of 16.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); NIST Joule definition
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 17, Potential Energy, pp. 455-456; NIST, joule definition

questions.stem: A powered carrier with a mass of 900 kg accelerates at 1.8 m/s^2. What net force produces this acceleration?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Newton second law gives F = m*a = 900 kg*1.8 m/s^2 = 1,620 N.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This divides mass by acceleration instead of multiplying.
This reports the mass as though it were already a force.
This uses 2.0 m/s^2 rather than the stated acceleration.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 17, Amount of Force and Newton second law, pp. 458-464

questions.stem: A 480 N load is 0.75 m from a fulcrum. What force applied 2.4 m from the fulcrum will balance the load?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Balance moments using F1*D1 = F2*D2. The required force is (480*0.75)/2.4 = 150 N.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This is the load-side moment, not the balancing force at 2.4 m.
This divides the load by the short distance and ignores the longer lever arm.
This multiplies the load by the long arm instead of balancing moments.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 17, Force and Distance, pp. 460-461

questions.stem: A 1,200 kg utility vehicle travels at 6.0 m/s. What is its linear momentum?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Momentum is p = m*v = 1,200 kg*6.0 m/s = 7,200 kg*m/s.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This divides mass by velocity rather than multiplying.
This applies an unnecessary one-half factor from the kinetic-energy equation.
This multiplies by velocity twice, which belongs to neither momentum nor the stated data.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)

questions.stem: A horizontal force of 350 N moves a crate 12 m in the same direction as the force. How much work is done?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: When force and displacement are aligned, W = F*s = 350 N*12 m = 4,200 J.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This adds the force and distance instead of multiplying them.
This doubles the force but does not account for the 12 m displacement.
This applies an unnecessary factor of two to the correct work.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); NIST Joule definition
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 17, Work, pp. 462-463; NIST, joule definition

questions.stem: A worker pulls a cart with a 500 N force at 30 degrees above horizontal for 8.0 m. Using cos 30 degrees = 0.866, how much work acts in the direction of travel?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Only the force component parallel to travel performs this work: W = F*s*cos(theta) = 500*8*0.866 = 3,464 J.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This applies an unsupported one-half factor to F*s.
This uses 0.80 rather than the given cosine value.
This uses all of F*s and ignores the angle between force and displacement.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); NIST Joule definition
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 17, Modified Work, pp. 463-464; NIST, joule definition

questions.stem: A cart is moving at 18 m/s and decelerates uniformly at 3.0 m/s^2. How long will it take to stop?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Use v = v0 + a*t. Setting final velocity to zero gives t = (0-18)/(-3.0) = 6.0 s.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Five seconds would leave the cart moving at 3 m/s.
Nine seconds would imply the cart continued accelerating backward after stopping.
This multiplies speed by deceleration instead of dividing the speed change by acceleration.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)

questions.stem: A maintenance cart starts at 4.0 m/s and accelerates at 2.5 m/s^2 over 24 m. What is its final speed?
incorrectOptionExplanations: This substitutes gravitational acceleration rather than solving the stated motion equation.
This adds the raw terms without taking the square root of the final squared velocity.
This reports v^2 as though it were velocity.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 17, Calculating Final Velocity, pp. 465-466

questions.stem: A suspended load pushes a tagline outward while the worker pulling the tagline feels an equal force in the opposite direction. Which principle best explains this interaction?
options: Newton first law: an object remains at rest unless acted upon by an unbalanced force.
Newton second law: acceleration equals net force divided by mass.
Newton third law: forces occur as equal and opposite interaction pairs.
Conservation of energy: mechanical energy can change form but is not created.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: The load and worker exert forces on each other as an action-reaction pair, equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
incorrectOptionExplanations: The first law addresses inertia, not the paired forces between two interacting bodies.
The second law relates net force, mass, and acceleration but does not define the equal-opposite pair.
Energy conservation concerns energy transformation and does not directly identify the interaction force pair.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 17, Newton Laws of Motion, p. 464

questions.stem: A calibrated test mass is moved from Earth to a location with lower gravitational acceleration. Which statement is correct?
options: Its mass and weight both increase because the object contains the same amount of matter.
Its mass decreases, while its weight stays constant because weight is an intrinsic property.
Its mass and weight both remain unchanged because neither depends on gravitational acceleration.
Its mass is unchanged, while its weight is lower because weight depends on local gravity.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Mass is the amount of matter and remains constant. Weight is gravitational force, W = m*g, so lower local gravity produces lower weight.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Keeping the same matter does not cause either quantity to increase; only weight varies with gravity.
Mass does not decrease when gravity changes, and weight is not constant across different gravitational fields.
Weight depends directly on gravitational acceleration even though mass does not.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 17, Defining Mass and Weight, pp. 458-459
questions.units: mass in kilograms; weight in newtons
